chief_complaint: stump shaping, phantom limb neuropathic pain management, and gait training in diabetic transtibial below-knee amputee
hpi_details: 58M diabetic 8 weeks post-transtibial amputation undergoing PM&R prosthetic fitting focusing on shrinker sock residual limb shaping, desensitization, neuropathic phantom pain titration with Pregabalin, and progressive parallel-bar prosthetic gait training.
ideas: He thinks the severed nerve endings at the bottom of his stump formed an inflamed knot that is misfiring pain signals.
concerns: He is worried that the burning pain means he will never be able to bear weight on an artificial limb and will remain confined to a wheelchair.
expectations: He hopes to adjust his nerve pain medication and get a clear timeframe for when he can start walking outdoors on his own.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Lower-Extremity Amputation Prosthetic Rehabilitation evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of lower-extremity amputation rehabilitation is essential for guiding safe prosthetic fitting and functional recovery.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Evidence-based diagnostic and therapeutic protocol for Amputation Lower Extremity Prosthetic Fitting, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

common_misconceptions: Assuming that phantom limb pain and residual-limb pain have the same cause.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Proceeding with prosthetic progression before confirming residual-limb skin integrity and volume stability.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Residual-limb infection, ischemia, or wound breakdown.

differentials: Peripheral arterial disease causing residual-limb ischemia

must_ask.say: Have you noticed any redness, drainage, skin breakdown, or worsening pain in your residual limb?
Do you feel painful sensations in the missing foot or leg, and what do they feel like?
Is your residual limb changing in size or making the socket feel loose or too tight?
Does wearing the prosthesis cause pressure areas, blisters, or pain?
What help do you need for transfers or walking, and have you had any falls?

history.answer: I had my below-knee amputation eight weeks ago, and I am here for residual limb shaping, control of my phantom nerve pain, and to start prosthetic gait training.
My right below-knee amputation was done eight weeks ago due to diabetic complications, and the healing has been progressing steadily since surgery.
I feel a strange tingling and burning sensation where my missing right foot and toes used to be, along with mild soreness at the very tip of my stump.
The phantom sensation feels like electric tingling or buzzing in the missing toes, usually about four out of ten in severity, while the stump itself is just mildly sore.
The phantom tingling comes and goes in short episodes several times a day, though it has become milder over the past couple of weeks.
Wearing my compression shrinker sock and doing gentle massage helps calm it down, but the phantom tingling tends to act up when I lie down quietly at night.
Besides the phantom tingling and mild stump soreness, I feel well and have no other pain.
I wear an elastic compression shrinker sock every day from morning to evening to help reduce swelling and shape the stump for a prosthesis.
It feels like my right foot is still attached and fallen asleep, with occasional pins-and-needles in the toes.
The incision has closed completely, and I have not seen any open sores, blisters, or drainage on my stump.
No, I have had no fever, chills, spreading redness, pus, or bad odor from the stump.
The skin on my stump stays warm, and I have not had any sudden coldness, severe throbbing rest pain, or dark discoloration.
I tried a preliminary socket fitting with the physical therapy team this week, and I did not feel any sharp pinching or excessive pressure.
I use a wheelchair and a walker to get around safely at home, and I have not had any slips or falls.
I gently rub and tap the tip of my stump with different fabrics each day, which has helped make the skin much less sensitive.
I need help getting into the shower and doing heavy household chores, and the nighttime phantom sensations occasionally disturb my sleep.
I had a right below-knee amputation eight weeks ago at this hospital, and the surgical staples were taken out three weeks ago without any issues.
I take lisinopril ten milligrams once daily, pregabalin seventy-five milligrams twice daily for the nerve pain, and metformin for my blood sugar.
The pregabalin has helped a lot by taking away the sharp, shooting nature of the phantom pain, leaving just mild tingling.
I have had type two diabetes for twelve years, high blood pressure for eight years, and mildly elevated cholesterol.
Other than my right below-knee amputation two months ago, I have never had any other surgeries or hospitalizations.
I do not have any known allergies to foods or medications.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco products.
I do not drink any alcoholic beverages.
I am a retired accountant living with my wife in a single-story house with no steps at the entryway.
My father had type two diabetes and high blood pressure, and my mother had hypertension.
I was wondering if the cut nerves down at the end of my stump got tangled into a painful knot that makes my missing foot feel like it's burning.
I'm terrified that this burning pain means my stump won't ever tolerate a prosthetic leg and I'll end up stuck in a wheelchair forever.
I'm hoping you can adjust my nerve pills so the burning eases up, and tell me when I can realistically expect to walk outside without these bars.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 128/78 mmHg, heart rate 74 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, body temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
Pleasant male seated comfortably in a wheelchair wearing a compression shrinker sock over his right lower extremity residual limb, appearing well and in no acute distress.
Right transtibial residual limb shows a mature, well-healed surgical incision without redness, warmth, dehiscence, drainage, or ulceration.

Residual limb displays mild cylindrical tapering with soft tissue tenderness on firm palpation over the distal surgical scar, without palpable neuroma or fluctuance; left calf is non-tender and supple.
Right knee demonstrates full active range of motion from zero to one hundred thirty degrees without flexion contracture, and all other lower limb joints have normal mobility.
Right femoral and popliteal pulses are 2+ and symmetric; left femoral, popliteal, dorsalis pedis, and posterior tibial pulses are intact with brisk capillary refill under two seconds.
Decreased light touch sensation on the left distal foot consistent with peripheral neuropathy, with mild superficial tingling sensitivity over the right distal residual limb.
Muscle strength is 5/5 in right hip flexion, extension, abduction, and right knee flexion and extension, as well as 5/5 throughout the left lower extremity.
Performs independent safe pivot transfers from wheelchair to exam table, and demonstrates good trunk control and static balance standing within parallel bars.
Regular rate and rhythm with normal first and second heart sounds; no murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
Lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally with normal vesicular breath sounds and no wheezes or crackles.
